lines.text: Where's your homework? You look up at Mr. Hollis.
You didn't do it. You were playing games until two in the morning.
So, you say the oldest lie in the world.
Sorry, sir. My dog ate it.
The whole class laughs.
Because everyone knows you don't have a dog.
That afternoon, you open your front door.
And there's a dog in your kitchen.
A big, brown, slobbery dog you've never seen in your life, sitting on the floor, chewing on your math homework.
Your mom walks in, rubs its head, and says, Did you feed biscuit today?
Biscuit. Your dog, who you've apparently had for six years.
There are photos of him on the fridge.
There's a leash by the door. There's a dent in the couch, the exact shape of him.
And everyone in your family remembers him.
Everyone except you.
Here's what you don't know yet.
Every lie you tell from now on is going to become true.
Every single one. And by the end of this year, you'll tell one lie so big that it erases the most important person in your life.
And the only way to bring them back will be the hardest thing you've ever had to say.
But first, biscuit needs a walk.
Most people lie about once or twice a day.
Small stuff. I'm fine.
I'm almost there. I love it.
Thank you. Scientists who study lying found that most of us tell a lie or two every day.
And a small group of people tell a lot of them.
You figure you're somewhere in the middle.
Then you start counting. And you realize you're not.
So you test it. Carefully.
At breakfast, your little sister Emma asks if you ate the last cookie.
You did. You say, no, there's more in the jar.
She opens the jar. It's full.
Full of cookies that weren't there five seconds ago.
At school, your friend Kai asks if you studied for the history test.
You didn't. You say, yeah, all weekend.
And then you sit down, look at the test, and you just know it.
Every date. Every name.
Like you really did study all weekend.
Because now you did.
You get a hundred. Then it gets fun.
Zoe sits by the window in English class.
She's never said a word to you.
Kai dares you to talk to her.
You walk over and say, hey, we met at summer camp.
Remember, you've never been to summer camp.
Zoe's face lights up.
Oh my gosh. Yes, you are the one who fell in the lake.
And suddenly you have a whole summer of memories together that you've never lived.
She remembers all of it. You remember none of it.
She asks if you want to sit together at lunch.
A guy cuts in front of you in the lunch line.
You say, actually, my dad owns this school.
By the next day, your dad owns the school.
He doesn't know how it happened. He's just suddenly the owner of a middle school, sitting in a meeting about cafeteria ketchup.
Very confused. At the mall, a shop assistant asks if you're old enough to buy a ticket to an R rated movie.
You say, I'm 18. You look down.
Your hands are bigger. You have a beard.
You walk into the movie. And when it's over, you say, just kidding.
I'm 14. And you're 14 again.
Kai saw the whole thing. He doesn't talk for an hour.
Then it gets bigger.
Your family has never had much money.
Your dad works two jobs.
Your mom counts coins at the grocery store.
So one night at dinner, you test the biggest lie you can think of.
You say, don't worry, dad's a millionaire.
The next morning, there's a new car in the driveway.
Your dad isn't working two jobs anymore.
He's running a company. He has an assistant.
He has a phone that never stops ringing.
Your mom cries when she sees the bank account.
You've never seen her look so relaxed.
You lie to a famous basketball player in a video comment.
You promise to come to my birthday.
Three weeks later, he's in your backyard, eating cake, saying, I really don't remember promising this, but happy birthday, man.
A TV reporter stops you outside school and asks what makes your town special.
You panic and say, we have the best pizza in America.
You don't. You have one pizza place and it's bad.
A month later, there are lines around the block, tourists from six states, and the owner is crying into a pile of dough, asking nobody in particular what changed.
Grandma knits you a sweater for your birthday.
It's orange and green, with a reindeer that looks like it's screaming.
You say what everyone says. I love it.
It's my favorite. And then you do love it.
Deeply, you wear it every day for three weeks in June.
Kids start asking where you got it.
You hear yourself say, my grandma is a famous designer.
By Friday, grandma has a fashion line in Paris and a waiting list of eight months.
You start to feel like the luckiest kid alive.
You can have anything as long as you say it wrong.
But here's the thing about lies.
Even normal ones, they don't stay where you put them.
Scientists at a university in London once put people in a brain scanner and gave them the chance to lie for money.
At first, the part of the brain linked to emotion lit up every time they lied.
It felt bad. But the more they lied, the quieter it got.
Each lie felt a little less wrong.
And the lies got bigger. That's exactly what happens to you.
You stop noticing when you're lying.
And that's when things start going wrong.
Your dad, the millionaire, is never home anymore.
He works 18 hours a day.
He misses dinner, then the weekend, then Emma's birthday.
He used to fall asleep on the couch with Biscuit.
Now, Biscuit waits by the door every night.
You did that. You made him rich, but you never said he'd be happy.
Zoe tells you about the summer camp again and again.
The time you fell in the lake, the campfire songs, the night you watched the stars.
She loves those memories. And every time she brings them up, you feel sick.
Because they're fake. She likes a version of you that never existed.
You lie to your teacher that you're sick to skip a test.
You wake up the next day with a real fever.
You lie that you're fine so your mom doesn't worry.
The fever disappears. You realize you can't even tell yourself the truth anymore without changing it.
Then comes the worst night of your life.
Kai finds out. He sees you lie to a cashier and watches her register suddenly fill with money.
He grabs your arm outside the store.
Was it all you? The test?
Your dad? Zoe? You nod.
He goes white. Did you ever lie about me?
You haven't, but he doesn't believe you.
He says you're not his friend.
You're just a guy who makes the world do whatever he wants.
And you're angry and you're scared and you shout the cruelest thing you can think of.
I don't even know who you are!
The second it leaves your mouth, you know.
Kai blinks. He looks at you like a stranger.
Sorry, he says politely.
Have we met? He walks away.
The next morning, his seat at school belongs to someone else.
His name isn't on the class list.
His mom doesn't remember he was ever friends with you.
In your phone, nine years of messages are gone.
Your photos from every birthday since second grade have someone missing in them.
A gap where a person should be.
You try to fix it. You say, Kai is my best friend.
But Kai doesn't appear. Because the power only works on lies.
And that sentence was true. It was always true.
You just lied the other way. For the first time, you understand how the power really works.
It doesn't give you what you want.
It gives you what you say.
And you can't take back a lie with the truth.
Only with another lie.
So you sit on your bed with biscuits head on your knee.
And you think, what lie could bring Kai back?
Kai remembers me. That would make him remember.
But then what? He'd remember every lie.
The fake test, the fake dad, the fake summer.
He'd remember that his best friend erased him from the world.
You'd get him back and lose him at the same time.
Unless. Unless you tell one more lie.
The biggest one you've ever told.
One that undoes all the others.
You'd lose everything. The money.
Zoe's memories. The basketball player's birthday visit.
Your dad's company. Biscuit.
You look down at biscuit. He wags his tail.
He doesn't know what you're about to do.
Of all the lies, he's the only one that made everyone happier.
And he has to go too. You walk downstairs.
Your dad is on the phone in his office.
At midnight. Again.
Emma is asleep on the couch, waiting up for him.
Your mom is reading the news on her phone about a family who woke up rich and doesn't know why.
You hug her. She asks what's wrong.
You almost say nothing.
You stop yourself. You've learned that much.
Then you go back to your room, look at the ceiling, and tell the biggest lie of your life.
I've never told a single lie.
Everything goes quiet. Where's your homework?
You look up. Mr. Hollis is standing over your desk.
It's that day again. The first day.
Your homework isn't done. You were playing games until two in the morning.
And next to you, in the seat that was empty yesterday, is Kai, chewing a pen, rolling his eyes at you, like always.
The whole class is waiting.
You open your mouth to say it.
My dog ate it. And you don't.
I didn't do it, sir. I was playing games.
I'm sorry. The class goes silent.
Nobody tells the truth about homework.
Mr. Hollis blinks. Well, he says.
Detention. But thank you for being honest.
Kai leans over. You okay?
You look weird. You look at him for a long time.
Then you say, I'm really glad you're my friend.
He makes a face. That's the weirdest thing anyone's ever said to me.
But he's smiling. That night at dinner, your dad comes home from his second job, tired.
He falls asleep on the couch before dessert.
Your mom counts the coins for tomorrow's groceries.
Emma tells a long story about a bug she found.
Nothing is perfect. Everything is real.
Here's one more thing scientists found.
Most people only catch a lie about half the time, barely better than flipping a coin.
Which means most of our lies work.
We get away with them. And maybe that's the problem.
When a lie works, it doesn't feel like it changed anything.
But it always does.
It just changes it quietly.
On Saturday, you see Zoe at the park.
She doesn't know you. There's no summer camp.
No lake. No stars.
You walk over anyway. You don't lie this time.
You say, Hi, I'm the guy who sits behind you in English.
I've wanted to talk to you for a year, and I didn't know what to say.
She laughs. That's honest.
Then she moves over on the bench.
You walk home the long way, pass the shelter on the corner, pass the window with the puppies, and you stop.
There's a big brown dog in the window, older than the others, slobbery, sitting in the corner, looking at you like he's seen you before.
The sign on his cage says, Biscuit, needs a family.
You walk inside. The woman at the desk asks, Do you know him?
And for once, you can say it.
And it's completely true. Yeah, I really do.
So what's the first lie you'd tell if every lie came true?
And what's the one you'd never dare to say?
Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have told the truth to get your best friend back, hit like and subscribe for more What Ifs.
